rows.title: US–Canada trade war
rows.milestone: Whether a trade fight between neighbours is leverage or self-harm.
rows.close_condition: Both governments withdraw the tariffs imposed since August.

rows.title: US–Israel–Iran
rows.milestone: Whether a campaign of strikes is a policy with an end, or a war nobody has named.
rows.stakes: The central question is whether the strikes on Iran amount to a policy with a stated end or a war no one has formally declared. Congress, the president, and Israel each answer differently on who decides when it stops, and diesel buyers are already paying for the uncertainty.
rows.close_condition: A negotiated halt to strikes and retaliation lasting more than ninety days.

indicator.label: U.S. average retail price of on-highway diesel, weekly

beginnings.line: President Trump ordered U.S. bombers and submarines to strike Iran's Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan nuclear sites, joining Israel's war on Iran, and said Iran must now make peace.
President Trump announced major combat operations in Iran, launched jointly with Israel, saying the objective was to defend Americans by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime.

G7 leaders agreed to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel through the International Energy Agency over four months, with diesel front-loaded into the first 20 days.
President Trump signed an executive order at a Nebraska rally allowing highway use of red-dyed diesel and directing the Treasury to defer federal diesel tax payments through the end of 2026.

objects.title: Address to the Nation on United States Airstrikes on Iran
objects.author: Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration (Compilation of Presidential Documents; President Donald J. Trump)
objects.evidence_quote: The President spoke at 10:02 p.m. in the East Room at the White House.
objects.about: This first direct U.S. attack on Iran's nuclear sites set the pattern of strikes announced as completed that the administration later cited as the reason for the February 2026 campaign.

objects.title: Remarks Announcing Major Combat Operations in Iran in Palm Beach, Florida
objects.author: The American Presidency Project (UC Santa Barbara), President Donald J. Trump
objects.evidence_quote: Our objective is to defend the American people by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime, a vicious group of very hard, terrible people.
objects.about: This is the start of the war that Trump's Truth Social post skipped over and that the diesel price spike traces to.

objects.title: G7 Leaders' statement on global energy security and market stability
objects.author: G7 Leaders (published by the Prime Minister of Canada's Office, pm.gc.ca)
objects.evidence_quote: We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary.
objects.about: This is the allied stock release that came alongside the White House dropping a diesel export ban, the step Sullivan had urged.

objects.title: WHAT THEY ARE SAYING: President Trump Delivers Immediate Diesel Relief, Saving Americans Up to $100 Per Fill
objects.author: The White House
objects.evidence_quote: Last night, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order that immediately cuts diesel costs by authorizing highway use of tax-free dyed diesel and deferring the federal diesel excise tax through the end of the year.
objects.about: It is the order the story examines, and it defers rather than waives the tax because only Congress can eliminate a tax.

here: A strike campaign with no declared end now shows up as a monthly diesel bill for farmers.

rows.title: Venezuela, post-Maduro
rows.milestone: Whether a state can be rebuilt by the people who fled it.
rows.close_condition: A recognised government exercising control with international acceptance.

rows.title: Israel–Hezbollah, Lebanon
rows.milestone: Whether a border can be quiet without a settlement behind it.
rows.close_condition: A durable withdrawal and ceasefire holding more than one year.

rows.title: Gaza
rows.milestone: Whether there is a limit force cannot be argued past.
rows.close_condition: A permanent ceasefire with an agreed administration for the territory.

rows.title: Sudan civil war
rows.milestone: Whether a country can survive two armies that each believe they are the state.
rows.close_condition: A signed settlement between the SAF and RSF holding six months.

rows.title: Ukraine–Russia
rows.milestone: Whether borders can still be changed by force.
rows.stakes: The category turns on whether Russia can keep territory taken from Ukraine by force, and whether sanctions relief is a price Washington will pay for a settlement. It also asks who decides: a president offering diesel access, Republican senators resisting, or Germany and other European governments holding their own line.
rows.close_condition: A ceasefire or settlement recognised by both governments.

beginnings.line: President Biden signed Executive Order 14066, banning imports of Russian crude oil, petroleum fuels and products of their distillation into the United States and barring new U.S. investment in Russian energy.
The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Rosneft and Lukoil, Russia's two largest oil companies, as blocked persons, the first major Russia sanctions action of Trump's second term.
The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License 133, temporarily authorizing sales of already-loaded Russian oil and petroleum products to India despite sanctions.

The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued Russia-related General License 135, authorizing sale, delivery and importation of Russian-origin diesel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027.

objects.title: Executive Order 14066: Prohibiting Certain Imports and New Investments With Respect to Continued Russian Federation Efforts To Undermine the Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity of Ukraine
objects.author: President of the United States (Joseph R. Biden Jr.)
objects.evidence_quote: Prohibiting Certain Imports and New Investments With Respect to Continued Russian Federation Efforts To Undermine the Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity of Ukraine
objects.about: It is the U.S. ban on Russian petroleum products, including diesel, that General License 135 now suspends for diesel.

objects.title: Treasury Sanctions Major Russian Oil Companies, Calls on Moscow to Immediately Agree to Ceasefire
objects.author: U.S. Department of the Treasury
objects.evidence_quote: Given President Putin's refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia's two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin's war machine.
objects.about: It is the Trump administration's own most severe energy sanction, which the diesel authorization of October 2026 partly walks back and which Republican critics cite.

objects.title: Issuance of Russia-related General License; Issuance of Amended Venezuela-related Frequently Asked Question
objects.author: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control
objects.evidence_quote: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is issuing Russia-related General License 133, "Authorizing the Delivery and Sale of Crude Oil and Petroleum Products of Russian Federation Origin Loaded on Vessels as of March 5, 2026 to India."
objects.about: It began the series of U.S. waivers easing sanctions on Russian fuel, the policy track from which the proposed Russian diesel deal grew and which Berlin and Republican senators resisted.

objects.title: Issuance of Russia-related General License
objects.author: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control
objects.evidence_quote: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is issuing Russia-related General License 135, "Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin."
objects.about: This license is the legal instrument behind the diesel deal that Republican lawmakers, GOP candidates and Chancellor Merz each publicly rejected or distanced themselves from.

here: A fuel-for-concessions offer met refusal from Republicans and Berlin before the day ended. The question was what Russia could be paid for.
Four Republican senators broke with the president on the plan. Four years in, the disagreement runs through Washington itself.

rows.title: Climate
rows.milestone: Whether long-term planetary risk warrants remaking how the country makes energy, or whether the remaking costs more than the risk.
rows.stakes: The question is how much we should change now to guard against a risk that is slow and spread out. One side sees a bill that grows the longer we wait. The other sees a bill we would pay today for a problem we can't yet price.

beginnings.line: Congress and President Nixon enacted the Clean Air Amendments of 1970, directing the new EPA to set standards for any air pollutant from new motor vehicles that endangers public health or welfare.
The Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 in Massachusetts v. EPA that greenhouse gases are air pollutants the EPA may regulate under the Clean Air Act and that Massachusetts had standing to sue.

The Supreme Court held in American Electric Power v. Connecticut that the Clean Air Act displaces federal common-law nuisance claims over power plant carbon dioxide, and left state-law claims for later.
Boulder County, San Miguel County and the City of Boulder filed suit in Boulder District Court against Exxon Mobil and Suncor affiliates, seeking to share the costs of climate impacts.
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5 to 2 that federal law does not preempt Boulder's state tort claims against Exxon and Suncor, and sent the case back to the trial court.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County and added a question on whether it has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear the case.

objects.title: Clean Air Act Amendments of 1970
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.evidence_quote: An Act to amend the Clean Air Act to provide for a more effective program to improve the quality of the Nation's air.
objects.about: Its Section 202 language became the statutory hook for federal greenhouse gas rules, and the later fight over whether that law displaces or preempts state suits is the core question in Boulder's case.

objects.title: Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.evidence_quote: Stevens, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, JJ., joined.
objects.about: It made the Clean Air Act the federal framework for carbon dioxide, which is the statute the oil companies now say displaces or preempts Boulder's state-law claims.

objects.title: American Electric Power Co. v. Connecticut, 564 U.S. 410
objects.author: Supreme Court of the United States
objects.evidence_quote: Argued April 19, 2011—Decided June 20, 2011
objects.about: It closed the federal common-law route for climate nuisance suits and left open the state-law question the Court is now hearing in Boulder's case.

objects.title: Complaint, Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County v. Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc., Case No. 2018CV030349
objects.author: Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County, Board of County Commissioners of San Miguel County, and City of Boulder
objects.evidence_quote: Alone, Plaintiffs and their taxpayers cannot pay the full costs of all that is needed, nor should they.
objects.about: This complaint is the lawsuit now before the Supreme Court, alleging that the companies' production and promotion of fossil fuels contributed to climate harms in Colorado.

objects.title: County Commissioners of Boulder County and City of Boulder v. Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc., et al., 2025 CO 21 (No. 24SA206)
objects.author: Colorado Supreme Court
objects.evidence_quote: JUSTICE SAMOUR, joined by JUSTICE BOATRIGHT, dissented.
objects.about: This is the decision Exxon and Suncor appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, and a 4 to 4 split among the eight participating justices would leave it standing.

objects.title: Order List (607 U.S.), Monday, February 23, 2026 — No. 25-170, Suncor Energy, Inc., et al. v. Commissioners of Boulder County, et al.
objects.author: Supreme Court of the United States
objects.evidence_quote: The petition for a writ of certiorari is granted.
objects.about: The grant put the case on the October 2026 docket, and the added jurisdiction question is why Justices Thomas and Jackson probed whether the case is ready for review.

here: The justices heard whether a Colorado county can bill oil companies for fire damage in its own state courts.

rows.title: The Media
rows.start_line: since Washington stopped requiring broadcasters to air both sides, August 1987
rows.milestone: Whether a democracy needs common facts from common institutions, or works better when citizens choose their own sources.
rows.stakes: If citizens can't agree on what happened, they can't argue usefully about what to do. Every rule about who may broadcast, publish, or be believed is a bet on how to keep that shared ground.

indicator.label: Trust the press a great deal or fair amount

objects.title: "The Themes of Muckraking"
objects.author: Walter Lippmann
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: "The Themes of Muckraking" is a piece written by Walter Lippmann in 1914. It discusses muckraking, the style of journalism that exposed wrongdoing. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: Abrams v U.S. SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Supreme Court decided Abrams v. United States on 10 November 1919. Defendants were convicted under the Espionage Act for leaflets thrown from a New York window that opposed sending troops to Russia and urged a strike in ammunition plants. The Court upheld the convictions. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes dissented, saying the leaflets posed no clear and present danger.

objects.title: Near v. Minnesota
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: Near v. Minnesota was decided by the U.S. Supreme Court on 1 June 1931. Minnesota had used a public nuisance law to shut down The Saturday Press, a Minneapolis paper that accused local officials of ties to gangsters. Chief Justice Charles Hughes wrote that the law was a prior restraint and violated the First Amendment. Four justices dissented.

objects.title: Telecommunications Act of 1996
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 is a federal law passed by the U.S. Congress and signed by President Clinton on February 8, 1996. It rewrote federal rules for telephone, cable, and broadcast companies, including limits on how many stations one company could own.

objects.title: Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: Reno v. ACLU was decided by the Supreme Court on 26 June 1997. It tested the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which made it a crime to send "obscene or indecent" messages online where minors could see them. The Court held that the Act violated the First Amendment as a content-based blanket restriction on speech. Justice O'Connor partly dissented.

beginnings.line: Walter Lippmann wrote an essay on the themes of muckraking, the reform journalism that exposed business and political corruption in the early 1900s.
The Supreme Court upheld the Espionage Act convictions of defendants who threw antiwar leaflets from a New York window, over a dissent by Justice Holmes.
The Supreme Court struck down Minnesota's law that let officials stop a newspaper from publishing, calling it a prior restraint under the First Amendment.

rows.title: Immigration
rows.start_line: since the last time Congress passed a big immigration law, November 1986
rows.milestone: Whether America renews itself through immigration, or must first settle who belongs and on what terms.
rows.stakes: Who comes in, and who gets to decide, shapes who the country becomes. People disagree about whether openness is what keeps America going or whether it needs clear terms first.

indicator.label: Foreign-born share of the population

objects.title: Chinese Exclusion Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Chinese Exclusion Act is a law passed by the U.S. Congress and dated 6 May 1882. It is found at 22 Stat. 58. The law limited immigration from China.

objects.title: Mexican Farm Labor Agreement
objects.author: United States and Mexico
objects.about: The United States and Mexico made this agreement on 4 August 1942 to let Mexican farm workers work in the United States for a set time. The linked text is the revision of 26 April 1943, made by an exchange of notes. It says Mexican workers could not be used in military service or face discrimination, and that employers would cover their transport and food.

objects.title: Plyler v. Doe
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: The Supreme Court decided this case on 15 June 1982. A 1975 Texas law let the state withhold school funds for educating children who were in the country illegally. The Court ruled that the law broke the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It said these children are people under that clause, and Texas had not shown a compelling interest, so it struck the law down.

objects.title: Immigration Reform and Control Act, signing statement
objects.author: Ronald Reagan
objects.about: On November 6, 1986, President Ronald Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act and issued a statement about it. He called it the most comprehensive reform of immigration laws since 1952. He said the act had three parts: penalties for employers, more enforcement, and legalization for some people already in the country.

objects.title: Arizona v. United States
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: In Arizona v. United States, decided June 25, 2012, the Supreme Court ruled on four parts of Arizona's 2010 immigration law, S.B. 1070. By a 5-3 vote, with Justice Kennedy writing, it held that federal law overrode three of them. It upheld the fourth, which lets state officers check immigration status during lawful arrests.

beginnings.line: Congress passed an act suspending the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States for ten years and fining ship masters who brought them.
The United States and Mexico agreed to recruit Mexican farm workers in Mexico for temporary work in the United States.
The Supreme Court struck down a Texas law that let the state withhold school funds for educating children who were in the country illegally.

rows.title: Faith
rows.start_line: since a preacher told Christians to organize as a voting bloc, June 1979
rows.milestone: Whether public life should stay secular and plural, or reflect a moral inheritance most Americans still hold.
rows.stakes: The argument is over whether shared public life should hold every belief at arm's length or reflect what most people already live by. It decides what a school, a courtroom or a holiday is allowed to say.

indicator.label: Adults with no religious affiliation

objects.title: Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
objects.author: Thomas Jefferson
objects.about: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom was written by Thomas Jefferson and dated 16 January 1786. It came from the Virginia General Assembly. It deals with religion and the freedom of belief.

objects.title: Reply to the Rev. Jacob Cram
objects.author: Red Jacket (Sagoyewatha)
objects.about: In November 1805, at a council at Buffalo Creek, the Seneca leader Red Jacket (Sagoyewatha) answered a missionary from the Boston Missionary Society. The missionary had said there was one right way to worship. Red Jacket replied that his people had their own religion from their fathers, asked why white people disagreed among themselves about theirs, and said the Seneca wished only to keep their own.

objects.title: Engel v. Vitale
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: In Engel v. Vitale, decided 25 June 1962, the Supreme Court ruled on a short prayer that the New York Board of Regents had approved for public schools each morning. Students did not have to take part, and the prayer named no particular faith. In an opinion by Justice Hugo Black, the Court held that the state could not hold prayers in public schools. Justice Stewart dissented.

objects.title: A Nation at Risk
objects.author: National Commission on Excellence in Education
objects.about: A Nation at Risk is a report issued in April 1983 by the National Commission on Excellence in Education. It was published by the U.S. Department of Education. It examines the state of American schools.

objects.title: Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: In Masterpiece Cakeshop, decided 4 June 2018, a Colorado baker named Jack Phillips had declined to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple because of his religious beliefs. Colorado's civil rights bodies ruled against him. The Supreme Court reversed 7 to 2. It held that commission members showed hostility toward his beliefs, which broke the Free Exercise Clause.

beginnings.line: Virginia's General Assembly passed a law, drafted by Thomas Jefferson, saying no one could be forced to support or attend any religious worship.
Red Jacket, a Seneca leader, answered a missionary from the Boston Missionary Society who had asked the Six Nations to accept his religion.
The Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not hold a prayer authorized by New York's Board of Regents, even though taking part was voluntary.

rows.title: Taiwan
rows.start_line: since Washington recognized Beijing and kept arming Taipei, January 1979
rows.milestone: Whether deliberate ambiguity is what has kept the peace, or what invites the miscalculation that ends it.
rows.stakes: The island sits where two nuclear powers' interests meet. Being unclear about what America would do may be what keeps the peace, or the thing that lets someone guess wrong.

indicator.label: PLA aircraft crossing the median line

objects.title: Formosa Resolution
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Formosa Resolution was a joint resolution of the U.S. Congress. It was passed on 29 January 1955. It authorized the President to use American armed forces to defend Formosa. It appears in the Statutes at Large.

objects.title: The Shanghai Communique
objects.author: USA and China
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Shanghai Communique was a joint statement by the United States and China, dated 27 February 1972. It dealt with relations between the two countries, including the question of Taiwan. Hofstadter included it in Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: Taiwan Relations Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Taiwan Relations Act is a law passed by the U.S. Congress and signed on April 10, 1979. It lets the United States keep commercial and cultural ties with the people on Taiwan after formal relations ended. It says the U.S. expects Taiwan's future to be settled peacefully, and that it will provide Taiwan with defensive arms.

objects.title: Anti-Secession Law
objects.author: National People’s Congress of the PRC
objects.about: The Anti-Secession Law was passed by China's National People's Congress on 14 March 2005. It is a Chinese law about Taiwan. Its text is published by the National People's Congress.

beginnings.line: Congress passed the Formosa Resolution on 29 January 1955, authorizing the President to use American armed forces to defend Formosa.
The United States and China issued the Shanghai Communique on 27 February 1972, a joint statement that addressed Taiwan among other subjects.
China's National People's Congress adopted the Anti-Secession Law on 14 March 2005, a law about Taiwan.

rows.title: Government
rows.start_line: since California voters capped their own property taxes, June 1978
rows.milestone: Whether government is the country's common instrument for security and opportunity, or the thing citizens must keep from growing too powerful.
rows.stakes: Americans want government to protect them, and also to leave them alone. Where that line sits decides who pays, who is covered, and who holds power over whom.

indicator.label: Trust Washington to do what's right

objects.title: Report on the Public Credit
objects.author: Alexander Hamilton
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this report for Congress in January 1790. It dealt with the debts the country had run up during the Revolutionary War. Hamilton argued that the federal government should pay those debts in full. He also proposed that the federal government take over the war debts of the states.

objects.title: First Annual Message to Congress
objects.author: John Quincy Adams
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The First Annual Message to Congress was delivered by John Quincy Adams on 6 December 1825. It is a message from the president to Congress. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: Munn v. Illinois
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Supreme Court decided this case in 1877. Illinois had set maximum rates that grain warehouses and elevators could charge. The owners said the rates denied them equal protection and due process under the 14th Amendment. The Court disagreed. Chief Justice Waite wrote that states may regulate private property "when such regulation becomes necessary for the public good."

objects.title: The Old Order Changeth
objects.author: William Allen White
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: William Allen White, a writer born in 1868 and dead by 1944, published this book in 1910. Its full title is The Old Order Changeth: A View of American Democracy. Macmillan of New York was the publisher. The Internet Archive copy, scanned from a University of California library, runs 288 pages and is filed under democracy and American politics and social conditions.

objects.title: Commonwealth Club Speech
objects.author: Franklin Roosevelt
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Commonwealth Club Speech was given by Franklin Roosevelt on 23 September 1932. It is a political speech about government. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: Confidential Memorandum: Attack on American Free Enterprise System
objects.author: Lewis F. Powell Jr.
objects.source: Memo to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Education Committee
objects.about: Lewis F. Powell Jr. wrote this confidential memorandum on 23 August 1971 for the Education Committee of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Its title is Attack on American Free Enterprise System. Washington and Lee University School of Law keeps it in the Powell Archives, in typescript and printed copies. The archive lists its subjects as commerce and free enterprise.

objects.title: Crisis of Confidence Address
objects.author: Jimmy Carter
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Jimmy Carter gave this televised speech on 15 July 1979, after ten days of meeting people at Camp David. He said he had planned to talk about energy but chose to talk about what he called a crisis of confidence. He said Americans were losing faith in the future and that a majority believed the next five years would be worse than the past five.

beginnings.line: Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton urged Congress to pay the national war debt in full and to have the federal government take over the states' debts.
President John Quincy Adams sent his first annual message to Congress on 6 December 1825.
The Supreme Court ruled that Illinois could cap rates charged by grain warehouses and elevators, since states may regulate property serving the public good.
William Allen White published The Old Order Changeth, a book about American democracy, issued by Macmillan in New York.
Franklin Roosevelt gave a campaign speech on progressive government to the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco.
Lewis Powell Jr. wrote a confidential memorandum to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Education Committee titled Attack on American Free Enterprise System.

rows.title: Order
rows.start_line: since gun owners took over their own lobby, May 1977
rows.milestone: Whether safety comes from stronger enforcement and armed self-reliance, or from limiting coercion and repairing what produces disorder.
rows.stakes: People want to feel safe, and they disagree about what makes that happen. One answer is more enforcement and the means to defend yourself. The other is less force and more attention to what breeds disorder.

indicator.label: Violent crime per 100,000 people

objects.title: National Prohibition Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The National Prohibition Act was passed by Congress and became law on 28 October 1919. Known as the Volstead Act, it set the rules for enforcing the national ban on making and selling intoxicating liquor. It also set penalties for breaking that ban.

objects.title: Miranda v. Arizona
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: Miranda v. Arizona was decided by the Supreme Court on 13 June 1966, by a 5-4 vote. Ernesto Miranda had confessed to police after two hours of questioning without being told of his right to a lawyer. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that suspects in custody must be warned that they can stay silent and have an attorney. Four justices dissented.

objects.title: Report on the Commission on Civil Disorders
objects.author: Commission on Civil Disorders
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Kerner Commission, formally the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, studied the causes of the civil disorders of 1967. Its report includes a history of Black Americans in American society and a city-by-city account of that summer's disorders. It also makes recommendations on police-community relations and on justice under emergency conditions.

objects.title: Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act is a federal law, Pub. L. 103-322, passed by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton on September 13, 1994. It covered many parts of crime policy. It paid for more police officers, banned certain semi-automatic firearms, and added more federal crimes that could bring the death penalty.

objects.title: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen was decided by the Supreme Court on 23 June 2022. New York required a person to show a special need for self-protection to get an unrestricted license to carry a concealed gun outside the home. The Court held that this rule violated the right to keep and bear arms in public for self-defense. Three justices dissented.

beginnings.line: Congress passed the National Prohibition Act over President Wilson's veto, setting out how the ban on alcoholic drinks would be enforced.
The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that police must warn suspects in custody of their right to remain silent and to have a lawyer before questioning.
The National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders issued a report on the 1967 civil disorders, with recommendations on police-community relations and social conditions.

rows.title: America Abroad
rows.start_line: since the last helicopter left Saigon, April 1975
rows.milestone: Whether American power should actively shape the world, or husband its strength and stay out.
rows.stakes: What America does overseas costs money and sometimes lives. The question is whether using that power makes the country safer, or whether holding it back does.

indicator.label: U.S. troops stationed abroad

objects.title: The Role of the Indians in the Rivalry Between France, Spain, and England
objects.author: Governor Glen
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Governor Glen of South Carolina wrote this account in 1761 of the Native nations near his colony. He listed the Catawba, Cherokee, Creek, Chickasaw and Choctaw, with rough counts of their fighting men. He said the colony's safety depended on staying friendly with them, and that this meant continuing to trade and give presents.

objects.title: Diary entry
objects.author: John Quincy Adams
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: John Quincy Adams, then Secretary of State, wrote this entry on 7 November 1823 after a Cabinet meeting at the President's. The Cabinet discussed a British proposal about European powers and South America. Adams argued the United States should not tie itself to Britain, and should state its own position to Russia and France instead. The meeting ended without a decision.

objects.title: Speech for Declaration of War Against Germany
objects.author: Woodrow Wilson
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Woodrow Wilson gave this address to a joint session of Congress on 2 April 1917 and asked for a declaration of war against Germany. He pointed to Germany's submarine warfare against ships. He said the country would fight for democracy and for the rights of small nations. Congress then voted, and the United States entered World War I.

objects.title: Press Conference on Lend-Lease
objects.author: Franklin Roosevelt
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Franklin Roosevelt held this press conference on 17 December 1940. He said the best defense of the United States was for Britain to succeed in defending itself. He proposed lending munitions instead of selling them for money, and compared it to lending a neighbor a garden hose to fight a fire. If the hose came back damaged, the neighbor would replace it.

objects.title: The Marshall Plan
objects.author: George C. Marshall
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave this speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947. He described the economic crisis in Europe after World War II and said the United States should help the region recover. He said the aid was aimed at hunger, poverty and chaos, not at any country. Europeans were to draw up a recovery plan and present it to the United States.

objects.title: First Inagural Address
objects.author: Richard Nixon
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Richard Nixon gave this speech when he took office as President on 20 January 1969. He spoke of a country at war that wanted peace and was divided and wanted unity. He said the world was moving from confrontation to negotiation, and that America's lines of communication would be open. He also asked Americans to lower their voices.

objects.title: Address on the Camp David Accords
objects.author: Jimmy Carter
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Jimmy Carter spoke to a joint session of Congress on 18 September 1978, after two weeks of talks at Camp David with Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menahem Begin. He described two agreements. One was a framework for peace in the Middle East. The other was a framework for a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel, which returned the Sinai Peninsula to Egyptian sovereignty.

beginnings.line: Governor Glen of South Carolina wrote that the colony's safety depended on staying friendly with the Indian nations against French influence.
John Quincy Adams wrote that Monroe's cabinet weighed British proposals about Spain and South America, and he opposed a joint pledge.
President Wilson asked a joint session of Congress to declare war on Germany after its submarines sank ships, and Congress then voted for war.
Franklin Roosevelt told reporters the United States could take over British munitions orders and lend or lease the goods, to be repaid in kind after the war.
Secretary of State George Marshall told Harvard graduates that the United States should help Europe recover from the war, through a plan the Europeans would draw up.
President Nixon said at his inauguration that the nation was moving from an era of confrontation to one of negotiation.

rows.title: Power
rows.milestone: Whether institutions should constrain elected power even when that means overruling what voters chose.
rows.stakes: Elected leaders answer to voters, and courts and agencies answer to the rules. When the two collide, someone has to give way, and the winner changes who really governs.

indicator.label: Say the other party threatens the nation

beginnings.line: The Constitutional Convention signed the Constitution, whose Article I, Section 6 shields members of Congress from being questioned elsewhere for legislative speech or debate and limits arrest during sessions.

The Supreme Court in Gravel v. United States held the Speech or Debate Clause protects legislative acts of members and aides from executive prosecution, but not conduct outside the legislative process.

The Justice Department applied for, and the FBI executed, the first search warrant on a sitting member's congressional office, that of Rep. William Jefferson, prompting a separation of powers challenge.

The D.C. Circuit held that the Justice Department's search of Rep. Jefferson's office violated the Speech or Debate privilege by exposing privileged legislative material to executive agents, while allowing the investigation to continue.

objects.title: The Constitution of the United States
objects.evidence_quote: They shall in all Cases, except Treason, Felony and Breach of the Peace, be privileged from Arrest during their Attendance at the Session of their respective Houses, and in going to and returning from the same; and for any Speech or Debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any other Place.
objects.about: It sets the constitutional baseline for how far the executive branch may go in investigating a sitting member of Congress such as Rep. Omar.

objects.title: Gravel v. United States, 408 U.S. 606
objects.author: Supreme Court of the United States
objects.evidence_quote: A grand jury investigating whether violations of federal law were implicated subpoenaed an aide to the Senator.
objects.about: It defines what the Justice Department may and may not pursue against a member of Congress, which frames any dispute over the Omar investigation.

objects.title: United States v. Rayburn House Office Building, Room 2113, Washington, D.C. 20515, No. 06-3105
objects.author: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit (copy hosted by the U.S. Department of Justice)
objects.evidence_quote: On May 18, 2006, the Department of Justice filed an application for a search warrant for Room 2113 of the Rayburn House Office Building, the congressional office of Congressman William J. Jefferson.
objects.about: It is the closest earlier case of the executive searching a sitting lawmaker's premises, and its court fight shows how Congress and courts test such searches.

objects.title: United States v. Rayburn House Office Building, Room 2113, Washington, D.C. 20515, No. 06-3105
objects.author: U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
objects.evidence_quote: Argued May 15, 2007 Decided August 3, 2007
objects.about: It established that a court may let an investigation of a member proceed while policing the line between legislative material and ordinary evidence, relevant to any challenge to the Omar warrant.

here: A judge-approved warrant reached a sitting member of Congress. The Justice Department decided that, and no voter did.

rows.title: Work
rows.milestone: Whether prosperity comes from freeing capital, or from restoring the bargaining power that once made a job enough.
rows.stakes: A paycheck used to be enough to build a life on, and many people feel it no longer is. The fight is over whether the fix is to free businesses to grow or to give workers more say.

indicator.label: Share of workers in a union

objects.title: "Of Colonies" from the Wealth of Nations
objects.author: Adam Smith
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: "Of Colonies" is a section of The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith. The book was published on 9 March 1776. The section discusses colonies and how they relate to the countries that rule them. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: South Carolina Protest against the Tariff of 1828
objects.author: S.C.
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The South Carolina Exposition and Protest was written in 1828 by John C. Calhoun, then Vice President, who kept his authorship hidden. It protested the Tariff of 1828 and said a state could reject federal law. It was presented to the South Carolina House on December 19, 1828. The legislature did not formally adopt it, but a pamphlet was printed.

objects.title: Populist Party Platform
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The People's Party adopted this platform at its first national convention on July 4, 1892. It describes a country in ruin, with money and land in the hands of a few. It demands a graduated income tax, free coinage of silver and gold at a ratio of 16 to 1, and postal savings banks run by the government.

objects.title: Cross of Gold Speech
objects.author: William Jennings Bryan
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Cross of Gold Speech was given by William Jennings Bryan on 8 July 1896. It is a political speech about money. It is reprinted in Hofstadter's Great Issues in American History.

objects.title: Address on the Economy
objects.author: Richard Nixon
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: On August 15, 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television to announce a new economic policy. He ordered a freeze on all prices and wages for 90 days. He added a 10 percent tax on imported goods. He also suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, which he called a defense against international speculators.

objects.title: Remarks on the Air Traffic Controllers Strike
objects.author: Ronald Reagan
objects.about: On August 3, 1981, President Ronald Reagan spoke to reporters after the air traffic controllers' union called a strike. He said federal workers had sworn an oath not to strike and that Congress had forbidden such strikes. He told controllers who did not report for work within 48 hours that they had forfeited their jobs and would be terminated.

beginnings.line: Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776, and the book included a chapter titled Of Colonies.
South Carolina's House of Representatives received an Exposition and Protest against the Tariff of 1828, written by John C. Calhoun, which threatened secession if the tariff was not repealed.
The People's Party of America held its first national convention on the Fourth of July and issued a platform describing a nation near ruin, with labor impoverished and land held by capitalists.
William Jennings Bryan gave the Cross of Gold speech on 8 July 1896.
President Richard Nixon told the nation he was ordering a 90-day freeze on prices and wages and suspending the dollar's convertibility into gold.

rows.title: Family
rows.start_line: since a president vetoed universal childcare, December 1971
rows.milestone: Whether raising children is a private family responsibility or a shared public one.
rows.stakes: Raising a child is expensive, tiring and hard to do alone. The question is whether that is a private matter for each family or a cost the whole country should share.

indicator.label: Median age at first marriage, women

objects.title: Keating-Owen Child Labor Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: Congress passed this law on 1 September 1916 to stop interstate shipment of goods made by child labor. It barred goods from mines and quarries that used children under sixteen, and from factories that used children under fourteen. Fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds could work no more than eight hours a day or six days a week. The Secretary of Labor could inspect workplaces.

objects.title: Hammer v. Dagenhart SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: The Supreme Court decided this case on 3 June 1918. Roland Dagenhart sued so his fourteen-year-old son Reuben could keep working in a textile mill, challenging the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act. Justice Day, for the majority, held the law invalid. He wrote that production is not commerce, and that the Tenth Amendment left regulating production to the states.

objects.title: Social Security Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: Congress passed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935, and President Franklin Roosevelt signed it. It set up a national program of retirement payments for older workers and a system of unemployment insurance run with the states. It also gave federal money to states to help needy children and other groups. It is recorded in the Statutes at Large at 49 Stat. 620.

objects.title: Veto of the Economic Opportunity Amendments
objects.author: Richard Nixon
objects.about: On December 9, 1971, President Richard Nixon vetoed S. 2007, the Economic Opportunity Amendments of 1971, which would have extended the anti-poverty law, created a National Legal Services Corporation, and set up a child development program. In his veto message he objected to the child development program on grounds including cost and a belief that it would move away from strengthening parental authority and involvement with children.

objects.title: Troxel v. Granville
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: Troxel v. Granville is a 2000 Supreme Court case (530 U.S. 57). A Washington law let any person ask a court for visitation with a child, and the paternal grandparents of two girls used it to seek more time than their mother, Tommie Granville, allowed. In a 6-3 decision, the Court held that the law violated parents' Fourteenth Amendment right to decide their children's care, custody, and control.

beginnings.line: Congress barred the interstate shipment of goods made in mines using children under sixteen, or in factories using children under fourteen.
The Supreme Court struck down the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act, ruling that production was not commerce and that regulating it belonged to the states.
Congress passed the Social Security Act, signed by President Franklin Roosevelt, creating national old-age insurance and federal aid to states for unemployment and dependent children.

rows.title: Equality
rows.start_line: since the Court ruled that separate could not be equal, May 1954
rows.milestone: Whether equal citizenship requires the law to act on inherited disadvantage, or requires the law to stop sorting people at all.
rows.stakes: Everyone agrees the law should treat people equally. The argument is whether that means acting on disadvantages people inherited, or refusing to sort anyone by group at all.

indicator.label: Black family wealth per $100 of white family wealth
indicator.source: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances

objects.title: Letter to Rev. Samson Occom
objects.author: Phillis Wheatley
objects.source: Printed in New England newspapers, spring 1774
objects.about: Phillis Wheatley wrote this letter on February 11, 1774, to Samson Occom, a Mohegan minister. Wheatley had been brought to Boston as an enslaved girl. She agreed with his reasons on the natural rights of Black people. She wrote that love of freedom is in every human breast. Newspapers printed it that spring.

objects.title: Franklin Hall address
objects.author: Maria W. Stewart
objects.about: Maria W. Stewart gave this lecture on September 21, 1832, at Franklin Hall in Boston. She was a free Black woman, and her audience included men, which was unusual for a woman speaker then. She called for civil rights for Northern Black people and questioned the push to send them to Africa. William Lloyd Garrison printed it in The Liberator.

objects.title: Speech in the Senate
objects.author: Stephen A. Douglas
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois gave this speech on January 30, 1854, in defense of his Kansas-Nebraska bill. The bill let people in the new territories decide for themselves whether to allow slavery. It also repealed the Missouri Compromise line. Critics had protested, and Douglas answered them on the Senate floor.

objects.title: The Wade-Davis Manifesto
objects.author: Wade - Davis
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Senator Benjamin Wade and Representative Henry Winter Davis published this open letter on 5 August 1864. They objected to President Lincoln's 18 July proclamation, which declined to sign their Reconstruction bill. They called his action an overreach of executive power and said Congress, not the President, should handle political reorganization of the rebel states.

objects.title: Slaughterhouse Cases - SCOTUS
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: In 1873 the Supreme Court ruled on a Louisiana law that gave one New Orleans company a slaughterhouse monopoly. Butchers who lost their trade sued under the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court upheld the law. It read the amendments as meant mainly to secure equality for former slaves and limited the Privileges or Immunities Clause to rights tied to the federal government.

objects.title: Executive Order 8802
objects.author: Franklin D. Roosevelt
objects.about: President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed this order on 25 June 1941. It barred discrimination by race, creed, color or national origin in defense industries and government work. It required defense contracts to include a no-discrimination clause and created a Committee on Fair Employment Practice to investigate complaints. Roosevelt issued it after labor leader A. Philip Randolph agreed to call off a planned march on Washington.

objects.title: Brown v Board of Education of Topeka
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court decided Brown v. Board of Education, which combined cases from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C. Black students had been refused admission to certain public schools under segregation laws. In a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Earl Warren, the Court held that separate schools were inherently unequal and violated the Equal Protection Clause.

beginnings.line: Phillis Wheatley wrote to the Rev. Samson Occom that she agreed with his reasons on the natural rights of Black people.
Maria W. Stewart spoke at Franklin Hall in Boston, calling for civil rights for northern Black people and questioning emigration to Africa.
Senator Stephen Douglas defended his Kansas-Nebraska bill on the Senate floor, arguing that each territory's people should decide the question of slavery themselves.
Ben Wade and H. Winter Davis published a manifesto attacking the President's July 18 proclamation on a bill he had not signed.
The Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana slaughterhouse monopoly, ruling that the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments were passed to give former slaves full equality.
Franklin Roosevelt signed an order banning racial discrimination in defense industry hiring and created a Committee on Fair Employment Practice to investigate complaints.

rows.title: Korea
rows.start_line: since the shooting stopped without a peace treaty, July 1953
rows.milestone: Whether an armistice meant to last months and lasting a lifetime is stability, or just a very long pause.
rows.stakes: The war stopped in 1953 with an armistice, not a peace treaty. Millions live under the threat of it restarting, and the question is whether this standoff is a stable peace or just a long pause.

indicator.label: Estimated North Korean nuclear warheads

objects.title: NSC-68: Objectives and Programs for National Security
objects.author: National Security Council
objects.about: NSC-68 is a report by the National Security Council dated 14 April 1950. Its title says it sets out objectives and programs for national security. It is published through The White House.

objects.title: Address to Congress
objects.author: Douglas C. MacArthur
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: General of the Army Douglas MacArthur gave this speech to a joint meeting of the House and Senate on 19 April 1951, in the House chamber. It was printed as Senate Document 82-36. The Library of Congress catalog lists its subjects as the Korean War, communism, and military readiness.

objects.title: Testimony on the Military Situation in the Far East
objects.author: Dean Acheson
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: Secretary of State Dean Acheson gave this testimony on 1 June 1951. It is part of Senate hearings by the Armed Services Committee, joined by the Foreign Relations Committee. The hearings looked at the Korean War, the reasons General Douglas MacArthur was recalled from his Far East command, and what the recall meant for the war.

objects.title: Korean Armistice Agreement
objects.author: U.N. Command, DPRK and PRC
objects.about: The Korean Armistice Agreement was signed on July 27, 1953, by the United Nations Command, North Korea and China. It stopped the fighting in the Korean War and set a military line with a demilitarized zone along it. It was a ceasefire, not a peace treaty.

objects.title: Joint Statement of the Singapore Summit
objects.author: United States and DPRK
objects.about: On June 12, 2018, President Donald Trump of the United States and Chairman Kim Jong Un of North Korea met in Singapore and issued a joint statement. In it, the two countries committed to build new relations and a lasting peace regime on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea committed to work toward complete denuclearization, and both sides committed to recover POW/MIA remains.

beginnings.line: The National Security Council delivered a report to President Truman setting out U.S. objectives and programs for national security.
General Douglas MacArthur spoke to a joint meeting of the House and Senate in the House chamber on April 19.
Secretary of State Dean Acheson testified to Senate committees in hearings on the Far East military situation and General MacArthur's recall.

rows.title: The Bomb
rows.start_line: since the first use of a nuclear weapon in war, August 1945
rows.milestone: Whether eighty years without a second use proves deterrence works, or only that we haven't run out of luck.
rows.stakes: No nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945. Some say that proves the threat of retaliation works. Others say it only shows we have been lucky so far.

indicator.label: Nuclear warheads worldwide

objects.title: Statement on the Bombing of Hiroshima
objects.author: Harry Truman
objects.about: President Harry Truman issued this statement on 6 August 1945, announcing that an American airplane had dropped one atomic bomb on Hiroshima, which he called an important Japanese Army base. He said the bomb had more power than 20,000 tons of TNT. He described the secret effort to build it, and warned that Japan could expect more destruction if it did not accept American terms.

objects.title: Report on Soviet Missiles in Cuba
objects.author: John F. Kennedy
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Kennedy gave this television address on October 22, 1962. He said surveillance had shown offensive missile sites being prepared in Cuba, built with Soviet help. He announced a strict quarantine on offensive military equipment shipped to Cuba, and said ships carrying such cargo would be turned back.

objects.title: Limited Nuclear Test Ban Treaty
objects.author: US, USSR and United Kingdom
objects.about: The United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom signed this treaty on 5 August 1963. It banned nuclear weapon tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. Tests underground were not covered. Other countries were later able to join it.

objects.title: Address on Arms Control Negotiations
objects.author: Ronald Reagan
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.about: President Ronald Reagan spoke to the National Press Club on November 18, 1981, ahead of arms talks with the Soviet Union set to open in Geneva on November 30. He offered to cancel the U.S. deployment of Pershing II and cruise missiles if the Soviets dismantled their SS-20, SS-4 and SS-5 missiles.

objects.title: New START Treaty
objects.author: United States and Russian Federation
objects.about: The New START Treaty is an agreement between the United States and the Russian Federation, dated 8 April 2010. It concerns the nuclear arms each country holds. It is published in the U.S. Treaties series.

objects.title: Nuclear Posture Review
objects.author: U.S. Dept. of Defense
objects.about: The Nuclear Posture Review is a Department of Defense report released in early 2018. The President ordered it on January 27, 2017. It says the nuclear forces need modernizing to keep a credible deterrent, and it calls the security situation more complex than any since the end of the Cold War.

beginnings.line: President Truman announced that an American plane had dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, a Japanese Army base.
The United States, Soviet Union and Britain signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air, in space and underwater.
Reagan offered to cancel new U.S. missiles in Europe if the Soviets dismantled their SS-20, SS-4 and SS-5 missiles.
The United States and Russia signed a treaty in Prague limiting each side's long-range nuclear weapons.
The Defense Department issued a Nuclear Posture Review, ordered by the President in January 2017, on keeping a safe and effective nuclear deterrent.

rows.title: Outbreak secrecy
rows.milestone: Whether a state that withholds or contradicts information during a suspected outbreak protects its public from panic, or endangers it by delaying the trust and cooperation containment depends on.
rows.stakes: When a government withholds or contradicts what it knows about a suspected outbreak, the open question is whether silence calms a population or wastes the weeks in which trust and cooperation decide whether containment holds. Who decides when to speak, and who gains from the delay, remain contested.

beginnings.line: The Soviet Union, the United States and the United Kingdom opened the Biological Weapons Convention for signature, with Article V obliging parties to consult and cooperate in solving problems under the treaty.
The United States raised the Sverdlovsk anthrax deaths with Soviet authorities in Moscow under Article V, and the Soviets replied that the dead had suffered intestinal anthrax from contaminated meat.
China's authorities officially reported 792 cases and 31 deaths of atypical pneumonia in Guangdong to WHO, after earlier reporting only 305 cases and 5 deaths, as a WHO team reviewed the data.
The World Health Assembly adopted resolution WHA56.28, asking the Director-General to take account of reports from sources other than official notifications and to validate them epidemiologically.

The 58th World Health Assembly adopted the International Health Regulations (2005), requiring each state to assess events in its territory and notify WHO within 24 hours of any that may constitute an international emergency.
WHO asked the Russian Federation for more information on the Irkutsk death under the International Health Regulations, after its monitoring picked up the media reports of suspected pneumonic plague.
Russian health authorities replied to WHO that no plague case had recently been reported in Irkutsk oblast and that about 200 contacts had been placed in quarantine.

objects.title: Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on Their Destruction
objects.author: States Parties to the Convention (depositaries: United States, United Kingdom, Soviet Union)
objects.evidence_quote: Signed at Washington, London, and Moscow April 10, 1972 Entered into force March 26, 1975
objects.about: Article V is the treaty channel through which Washington's pressure on Moscow over a lab death at a plague institute could be framed.

objects.title: 290. Memorandum of Conversation
objects.author: U.S. Department of State, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980, Volume VI
objects.evidence_quote: In responding to the USG demarche, the Soviets acknowledged that a number of deaths had occurred due to an anthrax epidemic in Sverdlovsk in April 1979, but asserted that it was the intestinal form of anthrax resulting from contaminated meat.
objects.about: It is the earlier case in which a Russian-state account of a lethal outbreak was contested by Washington, the pattern now repeating around Irkutsk.

objects.title: Disease Outbreak News: Data from China, countries introduce stringent control measures
objects.author: World Health Organization
objects.evidence_quote: Chinese authorities had previously reported to WHO, on 14 February, a total of 305 cases and 5 deaths from 16 November to 9 February 2003.
objects.about: It shows how a delayed and partial official count of an unexplained pneumonia shaped the international rules now invoked against Russia.

objects.title: Revision of the International Health Regulations (WHA56.28)
objects.author: Fifty-sixth World Health Assembly
objects.evidence_quote: to take into account reports from sources other than official notifications, to validate these reports according to established epidemiological principles
objects.about: It is the basis on which WHO acted on media reports of a plague death in Irkutsk before Russia had notified it.

objects.title: International Health Regulations (2005), Article 6 Notification
objects.author: World Health Organization, World Health Assembly
objects.evidence_quote: Each State Party shall assess events occurring within its territory by using the decision instrument in Annex 2.
objects.about: These are the rules under which WHO asked Russia to verify the Irkutsk death and which Tedros says require timely, complete and transparent reporting.

objects.title: WHO Director-General's opening remarks at the media briefing, 7 October 2026
objects.author: World Health Organization, Director-General
objects.evidence_quote: On Saturday, WHO asked the Russian Federation for more information, in accordance with the International Health Regulations.
objects.about: It is the formal outside demand for facts that Russian officials were meanwhile answering with contradictory statements and appeals against rumor.

objects.title: WHO Director-General's opening remarks at the media briefing, 7 October 2026
objects.author: World Health Organization, Director-General
objects.evidence_quote: Russian Federation responded, saying that no case of plague had recently been reported in the Irkutsk oblast, and that they had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.
objects.about: It is Russia's formal answer abroad, which names no cause of death and sits beside the domestic diagnosis of pneumonia of unknown aetiology.

here: Five regions are locked down and the cause of one death is still unstated. Containment is running ahead of explanation.

rows.title: Yemen war
rows.milestone: Whether Saudi air power and a rebuilt coalition can reverse the Houthi hold on Yemen, or whether a ground war the government cannot win will outlast every offensive announced.
rows.stakes: The question is whether Saudi air power, now backed by a pact with Turkey and Pakistan, can dislodge the Houthis from the north, or whether Yemen's government forces, unable to take and hold ground, will see every announced offensive stall. The answer decides who governs Sanaa, and who pays for the war.

indicator.label: People in Yemen requiring humanitarian assistance
indicator.source: UN OCHA, Yemen Humanitarian Response Plan 2019 (published on the UN in Yemen site)

beginnings.line: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2216, demanding that the Houthis withdraw from seized areas including Sanaa and imposing an arms embargo on Houthi leaders and forces loyal to Ali Abdullah Saleh.

The Yemeni government and the Houthis signed the Stockholm Agreement in Sweden, covering mutual redeployment from Hodeidah and its ports, a prisoner exchange mechanism, and a statement of understanding on Taiz.

President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, speaking from Riyadh, dismissed his vice president and irreversibly transferred his powers to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council chaired by Rashad al-Alimi.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Sharif signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Mecca, committing the three states to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.
UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg told the Security Council that the risk of large-scale conflict had become reality, as the Houthis launched a major offensive including on the port city of Mokha.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting of the Makkah Alliance for Defense committee in Riyadh, condemned attacks on the Kingdom, and appointed a Pakistani secretary-general for the alliance.

objects.title: Resolution 2216 (2015), S/RES/2216
objects.author: United Nations Security Council
objects.evidence_quote: Adopted by the Security Council at its 7426th meeting, on 14 April 2015
objects.about: It is the legal basis the government and coalition still cite for retaking Houthi-held territory, and the Council invoked it again in September 2026.

objects.title: Stockholm Agreement, annex to letter from the Secretary-General, S/2018/1134
objects.author: United Nations Security Council (transmitted by Secretary-General Guterres)
objects.evidence_quote: To fully implement this Agreement and to work towards the removal of any obstructions or impediments to its implementation.
objects.about: It is the last major negotiated arrangement over the Red Sea coast, where the Hodeidah naval strikes and the Mocha and Dhubab fighting now take place.

objects.title: A presidential announcement for transferring powers to a presidential leadership council
objects.author: Presidential Leadership Council of Yemen (Office of Rashad al-Alimi), publishing President Hadi's declaration
objects.evidence_quote: The presidential announcement for transferring powers and forming a presidential leadership council has been issued today.
objects.about: It created the body whose chairman, al-Alimi, announced the October 2026 offensive in a televised address.

objects.title: Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan Issue Joint Statement of the Makkah Al-Mukarramah Summit for Joint Defence
objects.author: Saudi Press Agency

objects.about: It is the Mecca Pact that Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activated after the Houthi offensive, and it is the basis for the rebuilt coalition in story 1.

objects.title: Briefing by the UN Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, to the Security Council
objects.author: Office of the UN Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen
objects.evidence_quote: That risk has now turned into a harsh reality.
objects.about: It records the Houthi advance toward Bab el-Mandeb that the government's October counteroffensive claims to have reversed.

objects.title: Joint Statement on the Emergency Meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the Makkah Alliance for Defense, 5 October 2026
objects.author: Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Foreign Affairs (joint statement of Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan)
objects.evidence_quote: The Parties also condemned in the strongest terms the attempted targeting of Makkah and Madinah, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom, reaffirming their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity.
objects.about: This meeting first put the August Mecca Pact to work, moving Pakistani and Turkish forces toward Saudi Arabia as the government offensive against the Houthis began.

here: Saudi Arabia is betting a larger coalition and new partners can break a stalemate the last coalition could not.

rows.title: AI
rows.milestone: Whether the companies building AI should answer for the harm it causes, or whether its benefits justify letting society absorb some of that harm.
rows.stakes: The question is whether AI companies should answer for the injuries their products cause, or whether the gains justify leaving patients and the public to absorb some of the damage. State legislatures, regulators, and executives are settling it now, in who gets to deploy AI and who is held liable.

indicator.label: Share of U.S. adults who say the increased use of AI in daily life makes them more concerned than excited

beginnings.line: Utah's Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy announced a sandbox agreement letting Doctronic's AI renew existing prescriptions, the first state-approved program for an AI system to take part in medical decisions.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman in state court, the first state-led suit against the company, alleging ChatGPT was marketed as safe despite known risks.
